title: PAUL SAID TWO WOMEN, TWO SONS, TWO COVENANTS—BUT ONLY ONE LEADS TO FREEDOM. WHICH ONE ARE YOU LIVING UNDER?
paragraphs: PAUL SAID TWO WOMEN, TWO SONS, TWO COVENANTS—BUT ONLY ONE LEADS TO FREEDOM. WHICH ONE ARE YOU LIVING UNDER?

The shocking truth behind Hagar and Sarah in Galatians 4:21–31—and why you can spend your entire life trying to please God, only to discover that you have been living like a slave when Jesus already paid the price to make you free.
There is a kind of prison that does not have iron bars.
It has church pews.
Open Bibles.
Perfect attendance.
Hands raised during worship.
And a heart that quietly whispers, “God, have I finally done enough for You to love me?”
You pray, but still feel unworthy.
You repent, but wonder whether God has grown tired of forgiving you.
You serve, give, sacrifice, and try to become a better Christian. Yet somewhere beneath all that effort lives an exhausting fear.
What if I am still not enough?
And perhaps the most frightening part is that you have become so accustomed to carrying this burden that you have mistaken it for holiness.
But what if the burden you have been carrying is the very thing Jesus came to lift?
What if you have been living like a servant desperately trying to earn a place in a house where, through Christ, you have already been welcomed as a child?
Nearly two thousand years ago, the apostle Paul confronted this very problem.
And he did something extraordinary.
He reached into the ancient story of Abraham's family, brought two women into the center of his argument, and declared that their stories illustrated two radically different ways of relating to God.
Their names were Hagar and Sarah.
One was enslaved.
The other was free.
Both became mothers of Abraham's sons.
But Paul saw something in their stories that went far beyond family history.
He saw a warning about slavery disguised as religion.
And a breathtaking announcement about freedom through Jesus Christ.
Before we go further, there is something you need to understand.
This is not a story about God loving one wounded woman and despising another. It is about the danger of trusting human effort for what only God's promise can accomplish.
And if you have ever felt spiritually exhausted, ashamed of your past, afraid of failing God, or uncertain whether His grace could really be enough for someone like you...
Stay with this story.
Because the answer Paul gives may change how you understand your entire relationship with Jesus.
In Galatians 4:21, Paul begins with a question that sounds almost confrontational:
“Tell me, ye that desire to be under the law, do ye not hear the law?” (KJV)
He was speaking to believers who were being pressured to accept observance of the Mosaic Law, particularly circumcision, as necessary for their full standing among God's covenant people.
They had heard the Gospel.
They had been taught that Jesus Christ was crucified and risen.
They had received the message of justification by faith.
Yet influential teachers were persuading them that faith in Christ was not enough.
They needed something more.
A religious requirement.
A visible mark.
An additional qualification to secure their place in God's family.
And Paul was alarmed.
Not because obedience was unimportant.
Not because God's commandments were evil.
But because they were being tempted to make law observance the basis of an acceptance that Christ had already secured through His redeeming work.
There is a difference between obeying God because you belong to Him and trying to obey God so that He will finally accept you.
One grows from grace.
The other attempts to purchase what grace alone can give.
And that distinction is where Paul's argument begins to cut into the human heart.
He takes his readers back to Genesis.
Back to Abraham.
Back to a promise that seemed humanly impossible.
God had promised Abraham descendants.
But years passed.
His wife Sarah remained unable to conceive.
The waiting became painful.
The promise remained.
The circumstances appeared to contradict it.
Imagine Sarah watching another year disappear.
Another season.
Another reminder that her body was aging while the child she longed for had not arrived.
Imagine Abraham remembering God's promise while looking at the impossibility surrounding him.
They believed God had spoken.
But they struggled with the waiting.
And when waiting became unbearable, Sarah proposed a human solution.
In Genesis 16, she gave her Egyptian servant Hagar to Abraham so that he might have a child through her, according to a practice known in their ancient world.
Hagar conceived.
And Ishmael was born.
But the arrangement brought conflict, humiliation, and suffering into an already complicated household.
Hagar was not merely a symbol in a theological argument.
She was a real woman.
An Egyptian servant with limited power over her circumstances.
A woman who suffered mistreatment.
A mother who knew what it meant to be vulnerable.
And here is something we must never forget when reading Paul's later illustration.
God did not ignore Hagar.
When she fled into the wilderness, the angel of the LORD encountered her.
Genesis 16:13 records her response:
“Thou God seest me.” (KJV)
The Hebrew expression associated with her confession is אֵל רֳאִי — ʾEl Roʾi, commonly understood as “God who sees me,” though the precise nuance of the phrase is discussed by translators.
Think about that.
Before Paul ever used Hagar's situation to illustrate slavery under a covenant, Genesis had already shown us that the Lord saw this suffering woman.
He heard her affliction.
He gave promises concerning her son.
And later, in Genesis 21, God again heard the boy's voice and provided for Hagar and Ishmael in the wilderness.
This matters deeply.
Because Paul's allegory must never be twisted into the claim that Hagar or Ishmael were worthless, hated, or beyond God's compassion.
Nor is Paul teaching that one ethnicity is inherently enslaved and another inherently free.
His argument concerns the source of covenant membership and the basis of righteousness before God.
And now the story turns.
Years after Ishmael's birth, God fulfilled His promise through Sarah.
Against every ordinary human expectation, Sarah conceived.
Isaac was born.
The promised son arrived, not because Abraham and Sarah had discovered the secret to controlling God's timetable, but because the Lord remained faithful to what He had spoken.
Genesis 21:1 says:
“And the LORD visited Sarah as he had said, and the LORD did unto Sarah as he had spoken.” (KJV)
Read those words again.
As He had said.
As He had spoken.
God did what God promised.
That is the heartbeat of the story.
And it is precisely what Paul wanted the Galatians to understand.
In Galatians 4:22–23, he writes:
The Greek text uses two expressions worth examining.
κατὰ σάρκα — kata sarka
Literally, “according to flesh.”
And:
δι’ ἐπαγγελίας — di’ epangelias
“Through promise.”
Here, “according to flesh” does not mean that Ishmael was inherently evil or that ordinary physical birth was sinful.
Paul is contrasting the ordinary human means associated with Ishmael's birth with God's extraordinary fulfillment of His promise in Isaac's birth.
That contrast becomes a picture of something far greater.
Human effort cannot manufacture God's saving promise.
And religious performance cannot replace dependence upon His grace.
Then Paul makes his startling declaration.
Galatians 4:24:
“Which things are an allegory: for these are the two covenants; the one from the mount Sinai, which gendereth to bondage, which is Agar.” (KJV)
The Greek word translated “are an allegory” is:
ἀλληγορούμενα — allēgoroumena
It refers to speaking of these events in a figurative or allegorical way.
Paul is not denying that Abraham, Sarah, Hagar, Ishmael, and Isaac were historical figures.
He is drawing a theological correspondence from their history.
He sees in these two mothers a picture of two covenantal realities.
Hagar represents Mount Sinai in his illustration, associated with the covenant under which Israel received the Law.
Sarah, though not named again in every part of the comparison, corresponds to the free woman and the Jerusalem above.
But here is where careful reading becomes essential.
Paul is not declaring that the Law was wicked.
He had already written in Romans 7:12:
“Wherefore the law is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good.” (KJV)
The problem is not God's holiness.
The problem is human sin.
The Law reveals God's righteous standard, but it cannot give sinful humanity the power to justify itself before Him.
As Galatians 3:21 makes clear, if a law capable of giving life had been given, righteousness would indeed have been by the Law.
But that is not what the Law could accomplish.
The Law exposes our need.
Christ provides the redemption we cannot achieve.
And when people treat obedience to the Law as the means of securing justification, they turn away from the sufficiency of Christ's work.
That is the bondage Paul is confronting.
Consider what this can look like in an ordinary Christian life.
You fall into a sin you promised God you would never repeat.
You feel ashamed.
You avoid prayer.
You stop opening your Bible because every page seems to accuse you.
You tell yourself you must first become spiritually presentable before returning to God.
Perhaps you even try to compensate by doing something religious.
An extra fast.
A longer prayer.
More service.
A larger donation.
Not as grateful expressions of love, but as attempts to make yourself acceptable again.
Yet the Gospel does not tell the repentant sinner to become worthy before approaching Christ.
It calls sinners to come to Christ because He alone can save them.
That does not make repentance optional.
It makes repentance possible without pretending we can save ourselves.
And it means your obedience is never the price of your adoption.
Jesus did not die so you could spend the rest of your life trying to earn what His blood purchased.
He died to redeem sinners.
He rose to give them life.
And through faith in Him, those who were far off are brought near.
Paul had already explained this in Galatians 3:13:
“Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us.” (KJV)
The Greek verb translated “redeemed” is ἐξηγόρασεν — exēgorasen, from a verb meaning to buy or redeem.
Paul's point is not that Christ paid a literal financial transaction to a human creditor.
It is that Christ acted decisively to deliver His people from the Law's curse by bearing that curse on their behalf.
The freedom of the Gospel is not cheap.
It was secured through the crucified Savior.
And now Paul's illustration becomes even more astonishing.
In Galatians 4:25–26, he contrasts the Jerusalem of his day, associated in his argument with bondage, with another Jerusalem.
“But Jerusalem which is above is free, which is the mother of us all.” (Galatians 4:26, KJV)
The Greek phrase is:
ἡ δὲ ἄνω Ἰερουσαλὴμ ἐλευθέρα ἐστίν — hē de anō Ierousalēm eleuthera estin
“But the Jerusalem above is free.”
The word ἐλευθέρα — eleuthera means “free.”
Paul is speaking of the heavenly Jerusalem, the reality associated with God's promise and the freedom of those who belong to Christ.
This is not a declaration that Jewish people are rejected by God because of their ethnicity, nor that Christians have permission to despise Jerusalem or Israel.
Paul himself was Jewish.
Jesus was Jewish.
The apostles were Jewish.
The Scriptures Paul used were Israel's Scriptures.
And Paul's concern throughout Galatians is that both Jews and Gentiles receive justification through faith in Jesus Christ, not through the works of the Law.
The dividing line is not race.
It is not ancestry.
It is not social status.
It is whether a person relies on Christ or seeks to establish righteousness through something else.
This is why Galatians 3:28–29 is so important.
In Christ, believers share one inheritance according to God's promise.
And that inheritance is not earned by possessing the right family name, religious résumé, or cultural background.
It is received through belonging to Jesus.
Perhaps you grew up in church.
Perhaps you know every worship song.
Perhaps people call you faithful.
Perhaps your family believes you are the strongest Christian among them.
But only you know what happens when the music stops.
Only you know how often you measure your worth by your performance.
Only you know the fear that rises when you fail.
And perhaps tonight, while reading this, you are beginning to realize something uncomfortable.
You have believed in Jesus.
But you have also been trying to make yourself your own savior.
Not by denying His name.
But by treating your goodness as the final guarantee of your acceptance.
That is an exhausting place to live.
And Paul wants you to see a better way.
He continues in Galatians 4:28:
“Now we, brethren, as Isaac was, are the children of promise.” (KJV)
Not children of flawless performance.
Not children of spiritual achievement.
Not children of religious superiority.
Children of promise.
What a beautiful expression.
The Greek is:
ἐπαγγελίας τέκνα — epangelias tekna
“Children of promise.”
The Christian's identity rests on God's gracious promise fulfilled in Jesus Christ.
This does not mean everyone automatically belongs to Christ regardless of faith.
Paul is addressing those who are in Christ, who have received the Spirit through faith, and who therefore share in the promised inheritance.
But for the believer who has been crushed by the fear of never being enough, these words are life-giving.
You are not saved because your hands have never been dirty.
You are saved by the One whose hands were pierced.
You are not justified because your past contains no scandal.
You are justified through faith in the Savior who bore sin and shame at the cross.
You are not adopted because you have finally become impressive.
You are adopted because God, in His grace, sent His Son to redeem those under the Law so that they might receive adoption as sons.
That is exactly what Paul had already written in Galatians 4:4–5.
And the next verse contains one of the tenderest declarations in the entire letter.
“And because ye are sons, God hath sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father.” (Galatians 4:6, KJV)
Ἀββᾶ ὁ πατήρ — Abba ho Patēr
“Abba, Father.”
Abba is an Aramaic form of address for father, retained in the Greek New Testament alongside its Greek equivalent.
It expresses a genuine filial relationship and personal address, not a magical formula or proof that God is merely a casual companion.
The astonishing truth is that through Christ, believers are brought into a relationship in which they may address God as Father.
Think about the difference.
The slave fears being thrown out.
The child has been welcomed into the family.
The person trying to earn salvation asks, “Have I done enough?”
The believer resting in Christ learns to say, “Father, thank You for what Your Son has done.”
And because the Father loves His children, He also disciplines and transforms them.
Grace is not permission to remain enslaved to sin.
It is the foundation of a new life in which the Holy Spirit produces obedience, holiness, and love.
You do not have to choose between grace and transformation.
True grace brings transformation.
Now we arrive at one of the most difficult parts of Paul's argument.
In Galatians 4:29, he writes:
Paul is drawing from the conflict surrounding Ishmael and Isaac, particularly the events of Genesis 21.
Genesis describes Ishmael's behavior toward Isaac using a Hebrew verb that can carry the sense of laughing, mocking, or playing, depending on context.
Paul interprets the conflict in light of the opposition experienced by those who belonged to Christ.
He sees a pattern: the child associated with ordinary human means stands in conflict with the child of promise.
But this must not become an excuse to demonize Ishmael, his descendants, or any people group.
Paul's purpose is to warn the Galatians about opposition to the Gospel of grace.
Then he quotes Genesis 21:10:
“Cast out the bondwoman and her son: for the son of the bondwoman shall not be heir with the son of the freewoman.” (Galatians 4:30, KJV)
Those are severe words.
And we must read them with care.
In Genesis, the expulsion of Hagar and Ishmael is a painful event in a broken household. God provides for them and preserves their lives.
In Galatians, Paul uses the passage to argue that the covenantal inheritance cannot be obtained through reliance on the Law instead of God's promise in Christ.
He is not commanding Christians to mistreat servants, reject vulnerable women, expel children, or persecute people who disagree with them.
He is declaring that the Galatians must not surrender their Gospel freedom to a system that makes Law observance the condition of justification.
That is the force of his argument.
You cannot add human merit to the finished work of Jesus and still treat His grace as sufficient.
And this is where the story reaches beyond first-century Galatia.
Because religious bondage does not always announce itself with the words “You must keep the Mosaic Law.”
Sometimes it sounds like this:
God will love me more if I never struggle.
God must be disappointed because my prayer life is inconsistent.
I cannot come back to church until I fix myself.
Maybe if I give enough, serve enough, and sacrifice enough, God will finally forgive my past.
Some of these thoughts may be wrapped in sincere desires for holiness.
But when they turn your obedience into the basis of your acceptance before God, they distort the Gospel.
Your prayers matter.
Your obedience matters.
Your generosity matters.
Your service matters.
Your repentance matters.
But none of them can replace the righteousness of Jesus Christ.
And none of them can purchase forgiveness.
You cannot outgive your guilt.
You cannot outwork your shame.
You cannot pay for your own redemption.
Only Jesus saves.
This is why Paul refuses to compromise.
He knows what is at stake.
If the Galatians accept the teaching that circumcision is necessary for justification, they are not merely adopting a harmless religious custom.
They are embracing a different basis for righteousness.
Paul warns them in Galatians 5:4 about seeking justification by the Law and falling away from grace.
And immediately afterward, in Galatians 5:1, he declares:
“Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.” (KJV)
There it is.
The command that rises out of the entire story.
Stand firm in the freedom Christ has given you.
Not freedom to sin without repentance.
Not freedom to disregard God's holiness.
Not freedom to exploit others.
But freedom from trying to establish your own righteousness before God.
Freedom to obey from love rather than terror.
Freedom to confess your sins rather than conceal them.
Freedom to return to the Father because Jesus Christ is your Advocate.
Freedom to live as someone redeemed by grace.
And perhaps this is the moment when the story becomes deeply personal.
Because some of us know what it is to live in a spiritual prison.
We have memories we wish we could erase.
Decisions we wish we could reverse.
Words we wish we could take back.
Some have hidden addictions.
Some have betrayed people who trusted them.
Some have walked away from God and are afraid to return.
Some have spent years appearing strong while quietly falling apart.
And some are carrying the terrible belief that their worst chapter has permanently disqualified them from God's mercy.
But listen carefully.
The Gospel does not deny the seriousness of sin.
It announces that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
He did not go to the cross because humanity was almost good enough.
He went because we could not rescue ourselves.
And He did not remain in the grave.
He rose again.
That means your past does not have to be your final identity.
Your failures do not have to be your final chapter.
Your shame does not have to become your permanent address.
Through repentance and faith in Jesus Christ, there is forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and the beginning of a transformed life.
Not because you have earned a second chance.
But because the Savior is merciful.
This is the beauty of our message:
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by erasing the need for confession, restitution, or repentance.
But by bringing guilty people to the cross, where forgiveness is found, and by giving them new life through the risen Christ.
And if you are reading this with tears in your eyes, wondering whether you can still come home...
The invitation of the Gospel is not to hide until you become worthy.
It is to turn to Jesus.
Confess your sin.
Trust His mercy.
Follow Him.
And allow His Spirit to reshape the life you once believed was beyond repair.
Perhaps you need to say something today that you have been too ashamed to say out loud.
Not to impress anyone.
Not to prove that you are spiritual.
But because you are tired of pretending.
Your words may encourage someone who believes they are the only person still struggling.
You do not need to disclose private details to be sincere. Sometimes a simple confession of dependence on Jesus is enough to remind another believer that they are not alone.
And please remember Hagar.
The woman whose story Paul used to illustrate bondage was also the woman whom God saw in the wilderness.
There is something profoundly comforting about that.
The God who sees the afflicted is the same God who fulfills His promises.
The God who heard Hagar's cry is the God who sent His Son into the world.
The God who kept His word to Abraham is the God who raised Jesus from the dead.
He has not become less faithful.
His grace has not become less powerful.
His Gospel has not become less sufficient.
And the answer to spiritual bondage is not to become more impressive.
It is to return to Christ.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a following around a personality.
Not to turn faith into a marketplace.
Not to make people feel that God's blessings can be purchased.

But to keep proclaiming the Gospel of Jesus Christ, to open the Scriptures faithfully, to encourage repentance and spiritual maturity, and to help people discover the transforming power of God's Word.
Every article we publish is meant to point beyond us.
To Christ.
To His cross.
To His resurrection.
To the truth that saves.

A single share may place this message before a family member who has stopped attending church, a friend who is silently questioning their faith, or someone who believes that God could never forgive what they have done.
You may never know who reads it.
You may never see their tears.
You may never hear their prayer.
But God's Word can reach people in moments you cannot see.
We want this community to become a place where Scripture is taken seriously, Jesus Christ is exalted, and people are encouraged to grow beyond surface-level inspiration into genuine discipleship.
These resources are part of our commitment to make biblical encouragement and spiritual nourishment more accessible.
It does not purchase forgiveness, salvation, spiritual status, or a greater share of Christ's love.
Those blessings cannot be bought.
But voluntary financial support can be a meaningful act of Christian generosity and stewardship when given freely, prayerfully, and according to one's ability.

Scripture teaches that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive material support for their work (1 Corinthians 9:14), and that giving should come from a willing heart rather than pressure or compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).

Whether you personally understand such giving as an offering or part of your broader stewardship, the important thing is that it comes from faith and love, not fear or the belief that God can be financially obligated.
These products can be useful reminders of biblical truth, but they are never substitutes for Scripture, prayer, fellowship, or a personal relationship with Jesus Christ.
Your sharing helps bring the message to more people.
Your prayers matter.
But before you leave, I want to bring you back to the two women with whom this story began.
Hagar and Sarah.
Two mothers.
Two sons.
Two covenantal realities in Paul's inspired illustration.
One associated with slavery.
The other with freedom.
And through their stories, Paul asks the Galatians a question that still confronts us today.
Where are you placing your confidence?
In what you can accomplish for God?
Or in what Jesus Christ has accomplished for sinners?
Because if your hope rests in your own performance, there will always be another failure to fear, another weakness to conceal, another achievement you think you must attain.
But if your hope rests in Christ, then even in your weakness, you can repent, return, and cling to the One whose grace is sufficient.
That is not spiritual laziness.
That is the beginning of true Christian freedom.
A freedom that produces love.
A freedom that leads to holiness.
A freedom that makes room for humble obedience because the question of how sinners are justified has already been answered at the cross.
So tonight, when the accusations return...
When your memories remind you of everything you wish you had never done...
When you wonder whether God has finally grown tired of you...
Remember the promise.
Remember the cross.
Remember the empty tomb.
And remember what Paul said:
“So then, brethren, we are not children of the bondwoman, but of the free.” (Galatians 4:31, KJV)
If you belong to Jesus Christ, do not return to the slavery of trying to justify yourself.
Stand firm in Him.
And if you have not yet trusted Him, the invitation remains: repent and believe the Gospel.
Because the most important question is not whether you have managed to make your life look religious.
It is whether you have come to the Savior who alone can make you new.
What has been harder for you—believing that God can forgive your past, or trusting that His grace is enough for your present?
Your answer may help another person find the courage to be honest before God.
And if you remember only one thing from this entire story, let it be this:
You were never meant to spend your life begging outside the door that Jesus opened through His blood.
